blocks.prompt: The Digger That Lifts With Oil
blocks.text: A digger is really called an excavator. Look at its arm. There are shiny silver tubes on it. Those tubes are full of oil. When the driver moves a lever, a pump pushes the oil hard into a tube. The oil pushes the arm. That is how the arm lifts. Oil makes the digger strong. The digger sits still to work. It does not drive forward to dig. It scoops, then the whole top spins around, and the bucket drops the dirt. Then it spins back. The bottom part with the tracks stays put.

blocks.prompt: Strong Because of Oil
blocks.text: A digger's real name is an excavator. It is not strong because of its engine alone. It is strong because of oil. Inside the excavator, a diesel engine turns a pump. The pump squeezes hydraulic oil into thin steel hoses. The oil travels to the shiny silver cylinders you can see on the boom. Oil is a liquid, but it barely squashes at all. When you push on trapped oil, it has nowhere to go, so it pushes right back. That push slides a piston out of the cylinder, and the piston shoves the arm. A small pump can move a very heavy arm this way. Look at the bucket. Each tooth comes to a point. The same push spread over a wide, flat edge would only smear the dirt. Pushed through a few sharp teeth, it cracks into hard ground instead. The teeth wear down, so they are made to unbolt and be swapped for new ones. The excavator does not drive forward to dig. It parks, digs a scoop, swings its whole top around, and empties the bucket. Then it swings back and does it again.

blocks.prompt: How a Digger Gets Its Strength
blocks.text: Call it a digger if you like. Its proper name is an excavator, and almost everything impressive about it comes down to trapped oil. A diesel engine sits inside the body. The engine never touches the bucket. All it does is spin pumps, and the pumps push hydraulic oil through steel hoses at enormous pressure. In a working excavator that oil can be pressed to around 5,000 pounds per square inch, well over a hundred times the pressure in a car tire. Oil barely compresses, so squeezed oil has only one way out: it shoves the piston inside a cylinder. Feed that pressure to a cylinder as wide as a dinner plate and the piston pushes with a force of several tons. Nothing is free, though. To move the heavy arm a short way, the pump must send a lot of oil a long way. You trade speed for strength. Now look at the back of the machine. That fat block behind the cab is a counterweight, and it is there for the same reason you lean back when you carry a heavy box. A loaded bucket hanging out front wants to tip the whole excavator onto its nose. The weight at the rear pulls the other way and holds it down. The tracks matter too. An excavator can weigh twenty tons, but that weight is spread across two long belts. Spread out like that, it presses on the ground more gently than a car tire does.

blocks.prompt: Pascal's Machine
blocks.text: The machine parked at the construction site has a nickname and a real name. Children call it a digger. Engineers call it a hydraulic excavator, and the first word is the one that matters. Digging machines are older than hydraulics. In 1839 a young American named William Otis patented the steam shovel, a boiler on a rail carriage that hauled a bucket through the dirt using steel cables and winches. Cable machines like it cut the railroads and the Panama Canal. They had one permanent weakness. A cable can pull, but a cable cannot push. To force a bucket into packed clay, those machines relied on the weight of the bucket and on clever linkages, and they were always fighting their own design. Hydraulics removed the problem. In 1951 a French company, Poclain, built the TY45, widely credited as the first fully hydraulic excavator able to swing all the way around. Its arm did not hang from a rope. It was driven, in both directions, by oil. The idea underneath is more than three hundred years old. Blaise Pascal noticed that pressure applied to a trapped fluid is passed along, undiminished, in every direction. Since force equals pressure multiplied by area, you can press gently on a small piston and get an enormous push out of a large one. The excavator lives on that bargain. A diesel engine spins pumps, the pumps raise the oil to thousands of pounds per square inch, and valves send it wherever the operator's joysticks ask. One quiet piece of engineering makes the whole thing possible. The upper body rotates endlessly on a toothed ring, yet the tracks below need oil too, and hoses would wind up and snap after a single turn. So the oil passes through a swivel joint at the center, a set of rotating seals that lets the top spin forever while the flow underneath never twists. Without that one part, a digger could only ever turn halfway around.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Pascal's principle, published in the 1600s
Roughly 5,000 pounds per square inch in the lines
Force = pressure x area, and you pay in distance
The counterweight supplies an opposing moment
Otis steam shovel 1839, Poclain TY45 1951
The swivel joint carries oil across a spinning joint

blocks.prompt: Trapped Oil and the Art of Not Falling Over
blocks.text: Watch an excavator work for a minute and you will notice it does something no other big machine bothers to do: it stays still. A truck drives. A bulldozer shoves forward. The excavator parks, plants itself, and then rearranges the world around it without going anywhere. Everything interesting about the machine follows from that decision. Start with the strength, because it is borrowed. The diesel engine buried behind the cab never touches the bucket, not through a gear, a shaft, or a chain. All the engine does is turn pumps, and the pumps do one job: they raise the pressure of hydraulic oil. In a working machine that oil is squeezed to something near five thousand pounds per square inch, well over a hundred times what is inside a car tire. Oil, unlike air, refuses to be compressed, so pressurized oil has exactly one option, and a piston is it. The principle is Blaise Pascal's, and it is more than three centuries old: pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout that fluid. Force is pressure multiplied by area, so the same oil that presses harmlessly on a narrow hose wall presses with tons of force on a wide piston face. This is a genuine bargain but not a free one. Energy is conserved, and the ledger balances in distance: to shift that heavy piston a few inches, the pump must move a great deal of oil. The machine buys force and pays in speed. That is why a digger's arm moves with such unhurried menace. It is not being careful. It is being honest about physics. Then there is the problem of not falling over. A bucket full of wet clay hanging out at the end of a long boom is a lever, and the load's turning effect grows with distance from the tipping point. The fat cast block behind the cab, the counterweight, is the answer: mass placed far enough back to generate an opposing moment. Reach too far with too heavy a load and the arithmetic loses, which is exactly why operators dig close and swing short, and why a machine that lifts many tons at its feet may be rated for very little at full stretch. The tracks solve a quieter problem. Twenty tons on four tires would sink into soft ground and stay there. Spread along two long belts, the same weight presses on any given patch of dirt more gently than a family car does through its tires. The teeth on the bucket run the same argument backwards: the machine wants pressure there, so it funnels an enormous force through a few hardened points, which is why they crack into ground a flat blade would only polish, and why they are bolted on to be replaced when they blunt. None of this was possible when digging machines ran on rope. William Otis patented a steam shovel in 1839, and cable excavators built the railroads and cut the Panama Canal, but they all shared one limitation: a cable can pull and a cable cannot push. They dropped their buckets and hoped gravity was enough. Hydraulics broke that ceiling. Poclain's TY45, built in France in 1951 and widely credited as the first fully hydraulic excavator with full rotation, could drive its arm down into clay as hard as it could lift it out. One last piece deserves credit. The upper house spins on a toothed ring without limit, yet the tracks below it also run on oil, and any hose crossing that joint would wind up and burst within a single turn. A swivel joint sits at the center, a stack of rotating seals that lets the top revolve forever while the oil beneath it never twists. It is the least dramatic component on the machine, and without it the digger would be a machine that could only ever turn halfway around.
